1.pericope_label: the command to number, after the plague

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch read the date as marking a sentence fully executed and explain why families are enumerated here and were not at Sinai — the land was to be divided among families; Ellicott takes the plague to have carried off the remnant of the older generation.

Calvin makes the census the proof of a promise kept, since after the loss of a whole generation the same number stands again, and notes that this was at least the third such count; Gill adds that it would show all the old generation dead but two.
Henry observes that Moses numbered only when commanded, unlike David, and that Eleazar is joined in the commission as Aaron had been, which confirmed his succession.

Clarke explains the count by the need to regulate the tribes and ascertain the proportion of land, the lots being disposed so that a numerous tribe should not draw a small inheritance; Wesley makes it a demonstration of God in both judgment and increase.

themes: take the sum of all the congregation
from twenty years old and upward
in the plains of Moab by Jordan near Jericho

5.pericope_label: Reuben, and the children of Korah who died not

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the Hebrew as making Korah perish in the earthquake but reports the Samaritan transposition that attaches him to the burning instead, and traces the tribe's loss to Dathan and Abiram drawing their own tribesmen in.

Calvin gives two reasons for inserting the story here, and makes the sparing of the sons a profound instance of unequal judgment — shoots raised from an accursed root, likely the authors of psalms; Gill takes the disputed words to mean the things belonging to Korah and places him at the tabernacle door.

Clarke resolves the difficulty about the children by a close reading of the earlier narrative, where only the families of Dathan and Abiram are named; Wesley reads the judgment as a monument set up against rebellion and against usurping the priesthood.

debates.question: Did Korah die in the earthquake or in the fire?
positions: Ellicott: the Hebrew as it stands makes him swallowed up with Dathan and Abiram
Clarke, Gill and Wesley: the Samaritan text and the sense both put him among the burnt, the words meaning the things belonging to Korah

themes: the sons of Pallu; Eliab
they became a sign
notwithstanding the children of Korah died not

schools.summary: Ellicott traces the collapse of Simeon to the chief offender at Baal-peor, and notes that this is the only tribe Moses left unblessed and that its inheritance was carved out of Judah's; Keil and Delitzsch account for the missing family and the variant spellings.
Gill registers the variant names in both tribes and passes on the rabbinic claim that the whole plague fell on Simeon, guessing that Gad's loss came in the presumptuous attempt on Canaan.
Wesley states the scale of the decrease and allows that names might be added or changed on occasions scripture does not record.

themes: the families of Simeon, two and twenty thousand and two hundred
the only tribe left unblessed
the children of Gad after their families

schools.summary: Ellicott explains the loss of all three southern tribes by their camping together and contaminating one another, and notes that Judah's two dead sons were replaced in the family list by grandsons.

Calvin makes the loss of two of Judah's sons the measure of the mercy, since from the two born of an incestuous connection grew the most numerous tribe in the register; Gill gives the same account of the substituted grandsons and of Issachar's four families.
Wesley marks the turn in the arithmetic, Judah being about two thousand more than before where every tribe named so far had been diminished.

themes: Er and Onan died in the land of Canaan
the families of Judah, threescore and sixteen thousand and five hundred
the sons of Issachar after their families

fidelity.note: The closing paragraph observes that the three southern tribes all shrank while the first two of the eastern camp both grew, and says so in the summary's own voice — it marks explicitly that no witness draws the contrast, and rests it on Ellicott's explanation of the southern losses. Every claim is traceable; the juxtaposition is not one any commentator makes.

26.pericope_label: Zebulun, and the house of Joseph divided

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch explain how the two sons of Joseph became founders of tribes by Israel's adoption, trace the eight families of Manasseh through a son and a grandson, and mark that the genealogy runs on to the five daughters in order to prepare for the legal question they would raise; Ellicott derives the grandson's name from his mother being an Aramitess.
Gill counts Zebulun's three families and its increase, and explains why Manasseh is named before Ephraim despite the birthright — the census figures, not the order of blessing.

themes: the sons of Zebulun after their families
Manasseh and Ephraim, the sons of Joseph
Zelophehad had no sons, but daughters

schools.summary: Ellicott notes that Moses renewed the prophecy of Ephraim's superiority at the very moment the numbers contradicted it; Keil and Delitzsch count the families of Ephraim and Benjamin as descending partly from sons and partly from grandsons.

Calvin sets the two brothers side by side and finds Jacob's prophecy begun but not yet fulfilled, the promised excellency deferred to a distant time; Gill records the missing sons of Benjamin and the variant spellings.
Wesley reads the increase of above twenty thousand in Manasseh as the fulfilment of what Jacob foretold of Joseph, and infers that the five missing sons of Benjamin were extinct.

themes: the families of Manasseh, fifty and two thousand and seven hundred
the families of Ephraim, thirty and two thousand and five hundred
the sons of Benjamin after their families

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch observe that Dan's descendants formed a single family and that this list gives only the leading families, smaller branches being passed over; they and Gill agree on the son of Asher who founded no family.

Calvin takes Dan as the standing case of a promise outrunning the family tree, since he was contemptible among his brethren and begat one son; Gill supposes the daughter named among Asher's descendants to have been remarkable, and reports the view that she was an heiress.
Wesley draws the comparison between Dan's one family and Benjamin's five and concludes that increase depends singly on God's blessing and good pleasure.

themes: these are the sons of Dan after their families
the children of Asher after their families
the name of the daughter of Asher was Sarah

48.pericope_label: Naphtali, and what the register shows

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch note that the four families of Naphtali tally exactly with the sons named in Genesis and in Chronicles, one of the few lists in the chapter that needs no explaining.
Gill places the tribe last because it stood under Dan's standard, and records the decrease of eight thousand.

Henry makes the whole register turn on the disproportion between stock and number — providence in building families does not tie itself to probabilities — and defines what family means here, a line rather than a household.

themes: the sons of Naphtali after their families
forty and five thousand and four hundred
the barren hath borne seven

fidelity.note: Two sentences are the summary's own cross-chapter observation rather than any witness's: that Naphtali, Zebulun and Dan are the only tribes whose family lists need no explaining, and that Naphtali's decrease alone is left without a cause while the other losses are laid to particular sins. Both are checkable against the chapter, but neither is stated by a commentator.

schools.summary: Ellicott passes on a reading of the decrease as comfort in affliction and warning in prosperity — a people who multiplied under persecution and were consumed in vanity after deliverance.

Calvin treats the total as the proof of his whole argument, the same number standing after six hundred thousand had fallen, and adds that the survivors were thereby warned not to fall away again; Gill keeps to what the sum counts.

Clarke sets the two censuses side by side tribe by tribe, notes that the camp proportions were preserved and the leading division strengthened for war, and passes on Ainsworth's count of fifty-seven families; Wesley compresses the sum into justice, mercy and truth together.

themes: six hundred thousand and a thousand seven hundred and thirty
a decrease of eighteen hundred and twenty since Sinai
fifty-seven families, and seventy souls that went down into Egypt

52.pericope_label: unto these shall the land be divided

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch state the rule of proportion and hold that each tribe was to receive a province called by its name for ever.

Calvin presses the demonstrative — unto these — as putting the land into the hands of the men just registered rather than a later generation, and as meant to make them bestir themselves; Gill explains the lot as keeping the division out of a magistrate's discretion.
Henry answers why so particular a register is kept — as they were multiplied so they were portioned, by promise — and reads the lot as reserving to God the appointing of the bounds of our habitation.

Clarke follows the word for the lot into its later senses, down to the naming of the clergy, and makes the divided land a figure of a greater portion; Wesley works out how lot and proportion were combined in practice, and how portions were adjusted between tribes.

themes: to many thou shalt give the more inheritance
the land shall be divided by lot
according to the names of the tribes of their fathers

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch explain both the separate count and the broken-off list, which turns aside to trace the descent of Moses and Aaron; Ellicott reports the alternative view that Jochebed was a remoter descendant of Levi and Amram a different man.

Calvin notes that the priestly line descends from the last-named son, reads the naming of a mother as an ingenuous confession of family dishonour rather than a boast, and sees in the survival of two priestly sons a providence on which the safety of the whole church hung; Gill goes through the gaps in the family list.
Henry observes that the tribe escaped the sentence precisely because it was not numbered with the rest, and that it had nonetheless grown by only a thousand.

debates.question: Who was Jochebed?
positions: Calvin and the plain reading: Levi's own daughter, so that Amram married his aunt
Ellicott reports the view that she was a granddaughter or remoter descendant, and Amram a different man from the son of Kohath

themes: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari
the name of Amram's wife was Jochebed
Nadab and Abihu died, when they offered strange fire

63.pericope_label: not a man left, save Caleb and Joshua

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch call the close a formula recording a penal sentence completely carried out; Ellicott weighs whether the exclusion covered Levi too and leaves the two considerations standing.

Calvin refuses to let the deaths be explained by ordinary mortality, since many had not reached their twenty-fourth year and some were younger than Caleb and Joshua, who lived on vigorously; Gill limits the comparison to the numbering of Israel and not of the Levites.
Henry finds righteousness, goodness and truth together in the result, and notes that the new generation were all of an age for service and had leisure in the wilderness to learn the law.
Wesley states flatly that the Levites did not share the judgment because they were not guilty of that sin.

themes: there was not a man of them whom Moses and Aaron numbered
they shall surely die in the wilderness
save Caleb the son of Jephunneh, and Joshua the son of Nun
